title: How the queen became the strongest piece in chess
description: For most of chess history the queen was one of the weakest pieces on the board, shuffling one square at a time. Then, around 500 years ago, players gave her the powers of rook and bishop at once — and the game exploded.

body.heading: The queen who could barely move
paragraphs: Chess began as a war game, and its 'queen' was originally a counsellor — a vizier in the Persian and Arabic versions — who could move exactly one square diagonally. Beside the rook, which swept whole ranks and files, the piece beside the king was a bodyguard, not a weapon.

Medieval European chess kept her weak for centuries. Games were slower, attacks took longer to build, and checkmate was a long siege rather than a sudden strike. The board's most famous piece spent a thousand years as one of its least powerful.

body.heading: The mad queen revolution
paragraphs: In the late 1400s, in Spain and Italy, players began trying a radical variant: the queen could move like a rook and a bishop combined — any distance, in any straight or diagonal line. Contemporaries called it 'mad queen chess', half scandalised, and it caught on like wildfire because it made the game dramatically faster and sharper.

The new queen changed everything downstream. Old openings were abandoned, checkmates could arrive in a handful of moves, and players had to defend from the very first turns. The chess the world plays today — the chess of the wooden pieces in front of you — is the mad queen's game.

takeaway: The chess queen spent a thousand years moving one square at a time; when players in the 1400s gave her the combined powers of rook and bishop, 'mad queen chess' became the modern game.
